content: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections and, in some cases, to prevent certain bacterial infections. It is not effective against viral infections such as the common cold or flu. This medication is typically taken orally, preferably on an empty stomach for optimal absorption, unless otherwise directed by a physician. Crushing the medication is not recommended due to its bitter taste, and it should be swallowed whole. The dosage and duration of treatment depend on the specific medical condition and the patient’s response to therapy. For best results, erythromycin should be taken at evenly spaced intervals. If prescribed for an infection, it is important to complete the full course of treatment, even if symptoms improve after a few days, to prevent the infection from returning. If used for prevention, it should be taken exactly as directed by the doctor. Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain or cramping, and loss of appetite. Taking the medication with food may help alleviate these symptoms. Rarely, erythromycin can cause a severe intestinal condition due to the bacteria Clostridium difficile (C. diff), which may occur during or even weeks to months after treatment. Prolonged or repeated use of erythromycin may lead to oral thrush or a new yeast infection. Severe allergic reactions to this drug are rare but possible. Erythromycin may cause a condition known as QT prolongation, which affects the heart rhythm and can increase the risk of serious irregular heartbeats. This risk is higher in individuals with certain medical conditions, low potassium or magnesium levels, or those taking other medications that can prolong the QT interval. It may also interfere with the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the typhoid vaccine. Some erythromycin products may contain sodium, which should be considered in patients on a sodium-restricted diet. The medication passes into breast milk, so caution is advised for nursing mothers. Drug interactions can alter the effectiveness of erythromycin or increase the risk of side effects. It is important to inform your doctor or pharmacist of all medications, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Erythromycin can slow the removal of other drugs from the body, potentially affecting their function. It may also interfere with certain laboratory tests, leading to false results. If a dose is missed, it should be taken as soon as remembered unless it is near the time of the next dose, in which case the missed dose should be skipped. The next dose should be taken at the regular time. Erythromycin should be stored at room temperature, away from light and moisture, and not in the bathroom. Expired or unused medication should be properly discarded. Erythromycin is primarily excreted by the liver, so caution is necessary when prescribing it to patients with impaired liver function. It has been associated with exacerbation of symptoms in patients with myasthenia gravis and has been linked to infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) in infants following therapy. Parents should be informed to contact their physician if vomiting or irritability with feeding occurs. Prolonged use may lead to overgrowth of non-susceptible bacteria or fungi, requiring discontinuation and appropriate therapy. In cases of bacterial infections, surgical procedures such as incision and drainage may be necessary alongside antibiotic therapy. Erythromycin is generally considered safe during pregnancy (Category B) and is compatible with breastfeeding, according to the American Academy of Pediatrics. However, it should only be used when clearly needed, and the benefits outweigh the risks.
